claim: Tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) significantly contributes to cancer progression.
source: Tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) significantly contributes to cancer progression.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data in this manuscript.

claim: Human cancer is enhanced by PPARγ loss-of-function mutations.
source: Human cancer is enhanced by PPARγ loss-of-function mutations, but inhibited by PPARγ agonists such as TZD diabetes drugs including rosiglitazone.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Human cancer is inhibited by PPARγ agonists such as TZD diabetes drugs including rosiglitazone.
source: Human cancer is enhanced by PPARγ loss-of-function mutations, but inhibited by PPARγ agonists such as TZD diabetes drugs including rosiglitazone.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Macrophage PPARγ deletion in mice exacerbates mammary tumor development.
source: Here we report that macrophage PPARγ deletion in mice not only exacerbates mammary tumor development but also impairs the anti-tumor effects of rosiglitazone.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Macrophage PPARγ deletion impairs the anti-tumor effects of rosiglitazone.
source: Here we report that macrophage PPARγ deletion in mice not only exacerbates mammary tumor development but also impairs the anti-tumor effects of rosiglitazone.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Gpr132 is a novel direct PPARγ target in macrophage.
source: Mechanistically, we identify Gpr132 as a novel direct PPARγ target in macrophage whose expression is enhanced by PPARγ loss but repressed by PPARγ activation.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assays and reporter assays shown in Figure 3H-J.

claim: Gpr132 expression is enhanced by PPARγ loss.
source: Mechanistically, we identify Gpr132 as a novel direct PPARγ target in macrophage whose expression is enhanced by PPARγ loss but repressed by PPARγ activation.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Gpr132 expression is repressed by PPARγ activation.
source: Mechanistically, we identify Gpr132 as a novel direct PPARγ target in macrophage whose expression is enhanced by PPARγ loss but repressed by PPARγ activation.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Macrophage Gpr132 is pro-inflammatory.
source: Functionally, macrophage Gpr132 is pro-inflammatory and pro-tumor.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Macrophage Gpr132 is pro-tumor.
source: Functionally, macrophage Gpr132 is pro-inflammatory and pro-tumor.
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 5I-K.

claim: Genetic Gpr132 deletion retards inflammation.
source: Genetic Gpr132 deletion not only retards inflammation and cancer growth but also abrogates the anti-tumor effects of PPARγ and rosiglitazone.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Genetic Gpr132 deletion retards cancer growth.
source: Genetic Gpr132 deletion not only retards inflammation and cancer growth but also abrogates the anti-tumor effects of PPARγ and rosiglitazone.
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Genetic Gpr132 deletion abrogates the anti-tumor effects of PPARγ.
source: Genetic Gpr132 deletion not only retards inflammation and cancer growth but also abrogates the anti-tumor effects of PPARγ and rosiglitazone.
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data in double knockout mice shown in Figure 5N.

claim: Genetic Gpr132 deletion abrogates the anti-tumor effects of rosiglitazone.
source: Genetic Gpr132 deletion not only retards inflammation and cancer growth but also abrogates the anti-tumor effects of PPARγ and rosiglitazone.
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 5L-M.

claim: Pharmacological Gpr132 inhibition significantly impedes mammary tumor malignancy.
source: Pharmacological Gpr132 inhibition significantly impedes mammary tumor malignancy.
evidence: This is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5O-P.

claim: Chronic inflammation is implicated in >15% of cancers.
source: Chronic inflammation is implicated in >15% of cancers (Coussens and Werb, 2002) and shown to promote tumorigenesis (Blaser et al., 1995; Kuper et al., 2000; Scholl et al., 1994; Shacter and Weitzman, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Coussens and Werb, 2002.

claim: Chronic inflammation promotes tumorigenesis.
source: Chronic inflammation is implicated in >15% of cancers (Coussens and Werb, 2002) and shown to promote tumorigenesis (Blaser et al., 1995; Kuper et al., 2000; Scholl et al., 1994; Shacter and Weitzman, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: TAM strongly correlates with poor cancer prognosis.
source: As a key player in inflammation and cancer progression, TAM strongly correlates with poor cancer prognosis (Bingle et al., 2002; Noy and Pollard, 2014; Qian and Pollard, 2010; Ruffell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Overexpression of macrophage colony-stimulating factor 1 (CSF1 or M-CSF) leads to accelerated tumor progression in mice and human.
source: For example, overexpression of macrophage colony-stimulating factor 1 (CSF1 or M-CSF) leads to accelerated tumor progression in mice and human (Lin et al., 2001; Scholl et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lin et al., 2001 and Scholl et al., 1994.

claim: TAM modulates therapeutic responses.
source: Moreover, TAM also modulates therapeutic responses (Ruffell and Coussens, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ruffell and Coussens, 2015.

claim: PPARγ loss-of-function mutations have been associated with human cancer development.
source: PPARγ loss-of-function mutations have been associated with human cancer development (Aldred et al., 2003; Sarraf et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aldred et al., 2003 and Sarraf et al., 1999.

claim: Synthetic PPARγ agonists, such as the TZD anti-diabetic drugs rosiglitazone and pioglitazone, have been implicated to inhibit tumor malignancy.
source: Synthetic PPARγ agonists, such as the TZD anti-diabetic drugs rosiglitazone and pioglitazone, have been implicated to inhibit tumor malignancy (Apostoli et al., 2015; Bosetti et al., 2013; Drzewoski et al., 2011; Feng et al., 2011; Fenner and Elstner, 2005; Fröhlich and Wahl, 2015; Kumar et al., 2009; Monami et al., 2014; Skelhorne-Gross et al., 2012; Uray et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The incidence of cancer malignancies was significantly lower in rosiglitazone-treated patients than in control groups.
source: Provocatively, a meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials reveal that the incidence of cancer malignancies was significantly lower in rosiglitazone-treated patients than in control groups, although rosiglitazone did not significantly modify the risk of cancer (Monami et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a meta-analysis by Monami et al., 2008.

claim: Rosiglitazone did not significantly modify the risk of cancer.
source: Provocatively, a meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials reveal that the incidence of cancer malignancies was significantly lower in rosiglitazone-treated patients than in control groups, although rosiglitazone did not significantly modify the risk of cancer (Monami et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a meta-analysis by Monami et al., 2008.

claim: Diabetes (especially type 2) correlates with higher risk of cancers including breast cancer.
source: Importantly, epidemiological studies suggest a bidirectional association between diabetes and cancer: diabetes (especially type 2) correlates with higher risk of cancers including breast cancer (Park et al., 2014; Smith and Gale, 2009, 2010); conversely, 8–18% of newly diagnosed cancer patients are diabetic, and cancer patients with preexisting diabetes are 50% more likely to die after surgery (Barone et al., 2010; Richardson and Pollack, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: 8–18% of newly diagnosed cancer patients are diabetic.
source: Importantly, epidemiological studies suggest a bidirectional association between diabetes and cancer: diabetes (especially type 2) correlates with higher risk of cancers including breast cancer (Park et al., 2014; Smith and Gale, 2009, 2010); conversely, 8–18% of newly diagnosed cancer patients are diabetic, and cancer patients with preexisting diabetes are 50% more likely to die after surgery (Barone et al., 2010; Richardson and Pollack, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barone et al., 2010 and Richardson and Pollack, 2005.

claim: Cancer patients with preexisting diabetes are 50% more likely to die after surgery.
source: Importantly, epidemiological studies suggest a bidirectional association between diabetes and cancer: diabetes (especially type 2) correlates with higher risk of cancers including breast cancer (Park et al., 2014; Smith and Gale, 2009, 2010); conversely, 8–18% of newly diagnosed cancer patients are diabetic, and cancer patients with preexisting diabetes are 50% more likely to die after surgery (Barone et al., 2010; Richardson and Pollack, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barone et al., 2010 and Richardson and Pollack, 2005.

claim: TZDs were shown to promote terminal differentiation, reduce proliferation and trigger lipid accumulation in human breast cancer cells and liposarcoma cells.
source: TZDs were shown to promote terminal differentiation, reduce proliferation and trigger lipid accumulation in human breast cancer cells and liposarcoma cells (Mueller et al., 1998; Tontonoz et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mueller et al., 1998 and Tontonoz et al., 1997.

claim: The anti-proliferative effect of pioglitazone was reported to involve a metabolic switch in lung and breast cancer cells.
source: More recently, the anti-proliferative effect of pioglitazone was reported to involve a metabolic switch in lung and breast cancer cells (Srivastava et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Srivastava et al., 2014.

claim: Female mice with PPARγ deletion in the hematopoietic and endothelial cells developed inflammation in their lactating mammary gland.
source: We previously reported that female mice with PPARγ deletion in the hematopoietic and endothelial cells developed inflammation in their lactating mammary gland. This led to the production of inflammatory milk, which triggered systemic inflammation in the nursing neonates manifested as a transient fur loss (Wan et al., 2007b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Wan et al., 2007b).

claim: PPARγ deletion in hematopoietic and endothelial cells led to the production of inflammatory milk, which triggered systemic inflammation in the nursing neonates manifested as a transient fur loss.
source: We previously reported that female mice with PPARγ deletion in the hematopoietic and endothelial cells developed inflammation in their lactating mammary gland. This led to the production of inflammatory milk, which triggered systemic inflammation in the nursing neonates manifested as a transient fur loss (Wan et al., 2007b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Wan et al., 2007b).

claim: Tie2Cre deleted PPARγ in hematopoietic cells and endothelial cells.
source: Tie2Cre deleted PPARγ in hematopoietic cells and endothelial cells as we previously described (Wan et al., 2007a, 2007b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: LyzCre deleted PPARγ in the myeloid lineage.
source: LyzCre deleted PPARγ in the myeloid lineage (Clausen et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Clausen et al., 1999.

claim: Tie2-g-KO mice confer a more complete macrophage PPARγ deletion (89%) compared with Lyz-g-KO mice (79%).
source: although Lyz-g-KO mice permit a more specific macrophage PPARγ deletion, Tie2-g-KO mice confer a more complete macrophage PPARγ deletion (89%) compared with Lyz-g-KO mice (79%).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement reported by the authors.

claim: Both Tie2Cre-induced and LyzCre-induced mf-g-KO mice showed enhanced tumor development as indicated by earlier onset and larger tumor volume compared to the littermate controls.
source: Compared to the littermate controls, both Tie2Cre-induced and LyzCre-induced mf-g-KO mice showed enhanced tumor development as indicated by earlier onset and larger tumor volume (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth measurements shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Staining for Ki67 and phospho histone H3 (PH3) in the tumor sections showed increased cell proliferation in mf-g-KO mice.
source: Staining for Ki67 and phospho histone H3 (PH3) in the tumor sections showed increased cell proliferation in mf-g-KO mice (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Py230 cell injection into the mammary fat pad showed that tumor growth was also exacerbated in mf-g-KO mice compared with control mice.
source: Py230 cell injection into the mammary fat pad showed that tumor growth was also exacerbated in mf-g-KO mice compared with control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The expression of pro-inflammatory genes was increased in tumor tissues, bone marrow cells and spleen cells from PPARγ-deficient mice, including COX-2, MMP9, MCP-1, TNFα and IL-1β.
source: The results showed that the expression of pro-inflammatory genes was increased in these PPARγ-deficient cells and tissues, including COX-2, MMP9, MCP-1, TNFα and IL-1β (Figure 1E–G) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-QPCR data shown in Figure 1E-G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The expression of M2 macrophage markers such as Arginase 1 was decreased in PPARγ-deficient cells.
source: In contrast, the expression of M2 macrophage markers such as Arginase 1 was decreased (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-QPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PPARγ deficiency promotes inflammatory macrophage activation but attenuates M2 phenotype.
source: These observations were consistent with previous reports from several laboratories including our own group that PPARγ deficiency promotes inflammatory macrophage activation but attenuates M2 phenotype (Odegaard et al., 2007; Ricote et al., 1998; Straus and Glass, 2007; Wan et al., 2007b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining using CD11b and F4/80 markers revealed enhanced TAM recruitment in both Tie2-g-KO and Lyz-g-KO mice compared with control mice.
source: Immunofluorescence staining using CD11b and F4/80 markers revealed enhanced TAM recruitment in both Tie2-g-KO and Lyz-g-KO mice compared with control mice (Figure 1H) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: PPARγ-deficient macrophages exhibit increased migration and CCR2 expression.
source: This is in line with previous findings that PPARγ-deficient macrophages exhibit increased migration and CCR2 expression (Babaev et al., 2005), whereas TZD treatment suppresses macrophage migration and CCR2 expression (Barlic et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2005; Han et al., 2000; Shah et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Babaev et al., 2005.

claim: TZD treatment suppresses macrophage migration and CCR2 expression.
source: This is in line with previous findings that PPARγ-deficient macrophages exhibit increased migration and CCR2 expression (Babaev et al., 2005), whereas TZD treatment suppresses macrophage migration and CCR2 expression (Barlic et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2005; Han et al., 2000; Shah et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: PPARγ agonists inhibit angiogenesis.
source: Consistent with the reports that PPARγ agonists inhibit angiogenesis (Goetze et al., 2002; Keshamouni et al., 2005; Scoditti et al., 2010), we found that the number of blood vessels in tumor sections was increased in Tie2-g-KO mice but unaltered in Lyz-g-KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–F), further indicating that PPARγ deficiency in macrophage alone is sufficient to augment tumor growth independent of changes in angiogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goetze et al., 2002; Keshamouni et al., 2005; Scoditti et al., 2010.

claim: The number of blood vessels in tumor sections was increased in Tie2-g-KO mice but unaltered in Lyz-g-KO mice.
source: Consistent with the reports that PPARγ agonists inhibit angiogenesis (Goetze et al., 2002; Keshamouni et al., 2005; Scoditti et al., 2010), we found that the number of blood vessels in tumor sections was increased in Tie2-g-KO mice but unaltered in Lyz-g-KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–F), further indicating that PPARγ deficiency in macrophage alone is sufficient to augment tumor growth independent of changes in angiogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: PPARγ deficiency in macrophage alone is sufficient to augment tumor growth independent of changes in angiogenesis.
source: Consistent with the reports that PPARγ agonists inhibit angiogenesis (Goetze et al., 2002; Keshamouni et al., 2005; Scoditti et al., 2010), we found that the number of blood vessels in tumor sections was increased in Tie2-g-KO mice but unaltered in Lyz-g-KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–F), further indicating that PPARγ deficiency in macrophage alone is sufficient to augment tumor growth independent of changes in angiogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Tie2-g-KO and Lyz-g-KO mice data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: Tumor cell proliferation was significantly augmented by PPARγ-deficient macrophages compared with WT control macrophages in co-culture.
source: The results showed that tumor cell proliferation was significantly augmented by PPARγ-deficient macrophages compared with WT control macrophages (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Co-culture with PPARγ-deficient macrophages led to an increased tumor cell colony formation.
source: Consistent with this observation, co-culture with PPARγ-deficient macrophages also led to an increased tumor cell colony formation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Co-culture with PPARγ-deficient macrophages resulted in higher expression of proliferation markers in cancer cells compared with WT control macrophages.
source: We found that co-culture with PPARγ-deficient macrophages resulted in higher expression of proliferation markers and lower expression of apoptosis markers in cancer cells compared with WT control macrophages (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-QPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Co-culture with PPARγ-deficient macrophages resulted in lower expression of apoptosis markers in cancer cells compared with WT control macrophages.
source: We found that co-culture with PPARγ-deficient macrophages resulted in higher expression of proliferation markers and lower expression of apoptosis markers in cancer cells compared with WT control macrophages (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-QPCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: PPARγ-deficient macrophages exhibited elevated expression of pro-inflammatory genes such as COX-2, MCP-1 and MMP-9.
source: In accordance with our in vivo observations (Figure 1), PPARγ-deficient macrophages exhibited elevated expression of pro-inflammatory genes such as COX-2, MCP-1 and MMP-9 but decreased M2 macrophage markers such as Arginase-1 (Figure 2F) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-QPCR data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PPARγ-deficient macrophages exhibited decreased M2 macrophage markers such as Arginase-1.
source: In accordance with our in vivo observations (Figure 1), PPARγ-deficient macrophages exhibited elevated expression of pro-inflammatory genes such as COX-2, MCP-1 and MMP-9 but decreased M2 macrophage markers such as Arginase-1 (Figure 2F) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-QPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PPARγ-deficient macrophages displayed higher levels of anti-apoptotic genes and lower levels of pro-apoptotic genes.
source: In addition, PPARγ-deficient macrophages displayed higher levels of anti-apoptotic genes and lower levels of pro-apoptotic genes (Figure 2G), indicating an augmented survival.
evidence: This is supported by RT-QPCR data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: PPARγ-deficient macrophages showed increased proliferation.
source: Moreover, PPARγ-deficient macrophages showed increased proliferation, measured by ATP content (Figure 2H) or MTT assay (not shown).
evidence: This is supported by ATP content measurement shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Cancer cell growth was significantly inhibited when co-cultured with rosiglitazone-treated WT macrophages compared with vehicle-treated WT macrophages.
source: The results showed that cancer cell growth was significantly inhibited when co-cultured with rosiglitazone-treated WT macrophages compared with vehicle-treated WT macrophages (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The rosiglitazone effect on cancer cell growth is macrophage-PPARγ-dependent because tumor cell proliferation was increased equally when co-cultured with PPARγ-deficient macrophages regardless of rosiglitazone or vehicle treatment.
source: Importantly, this rosiglitazone effect was macrophage-PPARγ-dependent because tumor cell proliferation was increased equally when co-cultured with PPARγ-deficient macrophages regardless of rosiglitazone or vehicle treatment (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Rosiglitazone induction of LXRα was observed in WT macrophages but not g-KO macrophages.
source: As a positive control, rosiglitazone induction of a previously reported PPARγ target gene LXRα (Chawla et al., 2001) was observed in WT macrophages but not g-KO macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-QPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and a citation to Chawla et al., 2001.

claim: The ability of rosiglitazone to suppress breast cancer growth was significantly attenuated in mf-g-KO mice.
source: The results show that the ability of rosiglitazone to suppress breast cancer growth was significantly attenuated in mf-g-KO mice (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The ability of rosiglitazone to reduce tumor-associated macrophages was impaired in mf-g-KO mice.
source: Consistent with this observation, the ability of rosiglitazone to reduce tumor-associated macrophages was also impaired in mf-g-KO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Tumor cell proliferation could be significantly enhanced by co-culture with PPARγ-deficient macrophages but not by the conditioned medium from PPARγ-deficient macrophages.
source: Our experiments reveal that tumor cell proliferation could be significantly enhanced by co-culture with PPARγ-deficient macrophages but not by the conditioned medium from PPARγ-deficient macrophages (Figure 3A–B), indicating that physical contact between macrophages and cancer cells may be required and thus the key tumor-modulating PPARγ target gene in macrophages likely encodes a membrane protein.
evidence: This is supported by co-culture and trans-well experiment data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Physical contact between macrophages and cancer cells may be required for the pro-tumor effects of PPARγ-deficient macrophages.
source: Our experiments reveal that tumor cell proliferation could be significantly enhanced by co-culture with PPARγ-deficient macrophages but not by the conditioned medium from PPARγ-deficient macrophages (Figure 3A–B), indicating that physical contact between macrophages and cancer cells may be required and thus the key tumor-modulating PPARγ target gene in macrophages likely encodes a membrane protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-culture and trans-well experiment data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The key tumor-modulating PPARγ target gene in macrophages likely encodes a membrane protein.
source: Our experiments reveal that tumor cell proliferation could be significantly enhanced by co-culture with PPARγ-deficient macrophages but not by the conditioned medium from PPARγ-deficient macrophages (Figure 3A–B), indicating that physical contact between macrophages and cancer cells may be required and thus the key tumor-modulating PPARγ target gene in macrophages likely encodes a membrane protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for physical contact shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Gpr132 was consistently and significantly upregulated in PPARγ-deficient macrophages compared with WT control macrophages.
source: Upon examining their expression in our macrophage cultures, we found that G protein-coupled receptor 132 (Gpr132, also known as G2A) was consistently and significantly upregulated in PPARγ-deficient macrophages compared with WT control macrophages (see below), whereas the expression of 11 other candidates was unaltered (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3E-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of 11 other candidate genes was unaltered in PPARγ-deficient macrophages.
source: Upon examining their expression in our macrophage cultures, we found that G protein-coupled receptor 132 (Gpr132, also known as G2A) was consistently and significantly upregulated in PPARγ-deficient macrophages compared with WT control macrophages (see below), whereas the expression of 11 other candidates was unaltered (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gpr132 was predominantly expressed in the hematopoietic cell types and tissues.
source: We found that Gpr132 was predominantly expressed in the hematopoietic cell types/tissues and highly expressed in macrophages, but largely absent in other tissues or tumor cells (Figure 3C–D), indicating that it may play an important role in macrophage function.
evidence: This is supported by RT-QPCR data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Gpr132 was highly expressed in macrophages.
source: We found that Gpr132 was predominantly expressed in the hematopoietic cell types/tissues and highly expressed in macrophages, but largely absent in other tissues or tumor cells (Figure 3C–D), indicating that it may play an important role in macrophage function.
evidence: This is supported by RT-QPCR data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Gpr132 was largely absent in other tissues or tumor cells.
source: We found that Gpr132 was predominantly expressed in the hematopoietic cell types/tissues and highly expressed in macrophages, but largely absent in other tissues or tumor cells (Figure 3C–D), indicating that it may play an important role in macrophage function.
evidence: This is supported by RT-QPCR data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Gpr132 may play an important role in macrophage function.
source: We found that Gpr132 was predominantly expressed in the hematopoietic cell types/tissues and highly expressed in macrophages, but largely absent in other tissues or tumor cells (Figure 3C–D), indicating that it may play an important role in macrophage function.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Gpr132 mRNA levels were significantly higher in PPARγ-deficient macrophages compared with control macrophages, either in macrophage cultures alone or in macrophages co-cultured with cancer cells.
source: Gpr132 expression was significantly higher in PPARγ-deficient macrophages compared with control macrophages, either in macrophage cultures alone or in macrophages co-cultured with cancer cells (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This is supported by RT-QPCR and western blot data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: PPARγ activation by rosiglitazone reduced Gpr132 expression in WT macrophages but not PPARγ-deficient macrophages.
source: In line with this observation, PPARγ activation by rosiglitazone reduced Gpr132 expression in WT macrophages but not PPARγ-deficient macrophages (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-QPCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: PPARγ represses Gpr132 expression.
source: These findings suggest that PPARγ represses Gpr132 expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing increased Gpr132 in PPARγ-deficient macrophages and decreased Gpr132 upon rosiglitazone treatment.

claim: Luciferase output from both 0.5 Kb and 1 Kb Gpr132 promoter was reduced by the co-transfection of PPARγ and further diminished by rosiglitazone treatment.
source: Transient transfection and reporter assays reveal that luciferase output from both 0.5 Kb and 1 Kb Gpr132 promoter was reduced by the co-transfection of PPARγ and further diminished by rosiglitazone treatment (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: PPARγ represses Gpr132 promoter via critical element(s) within the 500 base pairs upstream of Gpr132 transcription start site.
source: These results indicate that PPARγ represses Gpr132 promoter via critical element(s) within the 500 base pairs upstream of Gpr132 transcription start site.
evidence: This is inferred from the reporter assay data showing repression with both 0.5 kb and 1 kb promoters.

claim: A PPAR response element (PPRE) half site exists in the Gpr132 promoter region at position -188: CATCCGAGCAAGGTCAGAC.
source: Indeed, we identified a PPAR response element (PPRE) half site in this region (-188: CATCCGAGCAAGGTCAGAC).
evidence: This is a sequence identification reported by the authors.

claim: PPARγ could bind to the endogenous Gpr132 proximal promoter in macrophages but not an upstream negative control region.
source: Chromatin-immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay showed that PPARγ could bind to the endogenous Gpr132 proximal promoter in macrophages but not an upstream negative control region (Figure 3I); this binding was not significantly altered by rosiglitazone (not shown).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: PPARγ binding to Gpr132 promoter was not significantly altered by rosiglitazone.
source: Chromatin-immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay showed that PPARγ could bind to the endogenous Gpr132 proximal promoter in macrophages but not an upstream negative control region (Figure 3I); this binding was not significantly altered by rosiglitazone (not shown).
evidence: This is stated by the authors based on data not shown.

claim: H3K9Ac active transcription histone mark at the Gpr132 transcriptional start site was enhanced upon PPARγ knockdown and reduced by rosiglitazone in a PPARγ-dependent manner.
source: Moreover, ChIP assay revealed that H3K9Ac active transcription histone mark at the Gpr132 transcriptional start site was enhanced upon PPARγ knockdown and reduced by rosiglitazone in a PPARγ-dependent manner (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: PPARγ directly represses Gpr132 transcription in macrophages upon activation by either endogenous or synthetic ligands.
source: These mechanistic studies indicate that PPARγ directly represses Gpr132 transcription in macrophages upon activation by either endogenous or synthetic ligands.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data of reporter assays, ChIP assays, and gene expression analyses.

claim: Gpr132 expression in human macrophages derived from human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (hPBMN) was blunted by rosiglitazone.
source: Gpr132 expression in human macrophages derived from human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (hPBMN) was also blunted by rosiglitazone (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-QPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The PPARγ repression of Gpr132 is evolutionally conserved.
source: This indicates that the PPARγ repression of Gpr132 is evolutionally conserved and our findings in mice may translate to human physiology and disease.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that rosiglitazone reduces Gpr132 in both mouse and human macrophages.

claim: The findings in mice may translate to human physiology and disease.
source: This indicates that the PPARγ repression of Gpr132 is evolutionally conserved and our findings in mice may translate to human physiology and disease.
evidence: This is speculated based on the conservation of PPARγ-Gpr132 regulation between mouse and human.

claim: The Gpr132 expression in tumors mainly originates from hematopoietic cells in the microenvironment such as macrophages.
source: Because Gpr132 is highly expressed in human macrophages (Figure 4A) but absent in human breast cancer cells (Figure 3D), the Gpr132 expression in tumors mainly originates from hematopoietic cells in the microenvironment such as macrophages.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 4A.

claim: Compared with normal breast samples, the majority of breast cancer lesions displayed significantly higher Gpr132 expression.
source: Compared with normal breast samples, the majority of breast cancer lesions displayed significantly higher Gpr132 expression (Figure 4B); in addition, compared with ER-positive breast cancers, the more aggressive ER-negative breast cancers also exhibited higher Gpr132 expression (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Compared with ER-positive breast cancers, the more aggressive ER-negative breast cancers exhibited higher Gpr132 expression.
source: Compared with normal breast samples, the majority of breast cancer lesions displayed significantly higher Gpr132 expression (Figure 4B); in addition, compared with ER-positive breast cancers, the more aggressive ER-negative breast cancers also exhibited higher Gpr132 expression (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Human breast cancer tissues expressed significantly higher Gpr132 compared with normal breast control tissues.
source: Immunohistochemistry staining confirmed that human breast cancer tissues expressed significantly higher Gpr132 compared with normal breast control tissues (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Higher Gpr132 expression was significantly correlated with higher expression of pro-inflammatory markers including CCL2 (MCP-1), MMP9 and PTGS2 (COX-2) in breast cancer lesions.
source: Moreover, linear regression analyses showed that higher Gpr132 expression was significantly correlated with higher expression of pro-inflammatory markers including CCL2 (MCP-1), MMP9 and PTGS2 (COX-2) in breast cancer lesions (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by linear regression analyses of TCGA data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Macrophage Gpr132 may promote inflammation and tumor progression.
source: These findings further suggest that macrophage Gpr132 may promote inflammation and tumor progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between Gpr132 and pro-inflammatory markers in human breast cancer.

claim: Gpr132 knockdown in macrophages significantly reduced cancer cell growth in co-culture.
source: Gpr132 knockdown in macrophages significantly reduced cancer cell growth (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Gpr132 over-expression in macrophages increased cancer cell growth in co-culture.
source: Conversely, Gpr132 over-expression in macrophages increased cancer cell growth (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Gpr132-KO macrophages displayed lower pro-inflammatory genes compared with WT macrophages.
source: Gene expression analyses reveal that Gpr132-KO macrophages displayed the opposite phenotype from PPARγ-deficient macrophages, with lower pro-inflammatory genes (Figure 5G), higher pro-apoptotic genes and lower anti-apoptotic genes (Figure 5H) compared with WT macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by RT-QPCR data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Gpr132-KO macrophages displayed higher pro-apoptotic genes and lower anti-apoptotic genes compared with WT macrophages.
source: Gene expression analyses reveal that Gpr132-KO macrophages displayed the opposite phenotype from PPARγ-deficient macrophages, with lower pro-inflammatory genes (Figure 5G), higher pro-apoptotic genes and lower anti-apoptotic genes (Figure 5H) compared with WT macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by RT-QPCR data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Gpr132-KO macrophages exhibited a significantly reduced ability to promote cancer cell colony formation and growth in co-culture.
source: In vitro macrophage-tumor cell co-culture experiments showed that Gpr132-KO macrophages exhibited a significantly reduced ability to promote cancer cell colony formation and growth (Figure 5I–J).
evidence: This is supported by colony formation and luciferase assay data shown in Figure 5I-J.

claim: Gpr132 enhances inflammation and macrophage survival.
source: These results indicate that Gpr132 enhances inflammation and macrophage survival, and the upregulated Gpr132 in PPARγ-deficient macrophages may confer their tumor-promoting effects.
evidence: This is inferred from the gene expression and functional data in Gpr132-KO macrophages.

claim: The upregulated Gpr132 in PPARγ-deficient macrophages may confer their tumor-promoting effects.
source: These results indicate that Gpr132 enhances inflammation and macrophage survival, and the upregulated Gpr132 in PPARγ-deficient macrophages may confer their tumor-promoting effects.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing opposite phenotypes of Gpr132-KO and PPARγ-KO macrophages.

claim: Tumor growth was significantly diminished in Gpr132-KO mice compared with WT and Gpr132 heterozygous (Het) controls.
source: Compared with WT and Gpr132 heterozygous (Het) controls, Gpr132-KO mice exhibited significantly diminished tumor growth (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Gpr132-Het mice showed attenuated tumor growth at a later stage compared with WT controls.
source: Compared with WT controls, Gpr132-Het mice also showed attenuated tumor growth at a later stage (Figure 5K), indicating that Gpr132 regulation is dosage-sensitive.
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Gpr132 regulation is dosage-sensitive.
source: Compared with WT controls, Gpr132-Het mice also showed attenuated tumor growth at a later stage (Figure 5K), indicating that Gpr132 regulation is dosage-sensitive.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Gpr132-Het mice show intermediate tumor growth phenotype.

claim: Gpr132 inhibition may impede cancer progression.
source: Together, our in vitro and in vivo results indicate that macrophage Gpr132 promotes tumor growth, suggesting that Gpr132 inhibition may impede cancer progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing reduced tumor growth in Gpr132-KO mice.

claim: Pre-treating Gpr132-KO macrophages with rosiglitazone before cancer cell seeding no longer showed any inhibition of cancer cell proliferation in the co-cultures.
source: Pre-treating Gpr132-KO macrophages with rosiglitazone before cancer cell seeding no longer showed any inhibition of cancer cell proliferation in the co-cultures (Figure 5L) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 5L and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The anti-tumor effect of rosiglitazone in vivo was abolished in Gpr132-KO mice.
source: Consistent with this in vitro observation, the anti-tumor effect of rosiglitazone in vivo was also abolished in Gpr132-KO mice (Figure 5M).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: The PPARγ repression of Gpr132 in macrophages is a significant contributor to the anti-tumor effects of rosiglitazone.
source: These pharmacological findings support that the PPARγ repression of Gpr132 in macrophages is a significant contributor to the anti-tumor effects of rosiglitazone.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that rosiglitazone's anti-tumor effects are abolished in Gpr132-KO mice.

claim: Gpr132 deletion in the DKO mice impaired the ability of macrophage PPARγ deficiency to exacerbate tumor growth because DKO mice showed similar tumor volume as Gpr132-KO mice.
source: Mammary fat pad tumor graft experiments demonstrated that Gpr132 deletion in the DKO mice impaired the ability of macrophage PPARγ deficiency to exacerbate tumor growth because DKO mice showed similar tumor volume as Gpr132-KO mice (Figure 5N).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 5N.

claim: Gpr132 is an essential mediator of macrophage PPARγ regulation of breast cancer progression.
source: This genetic rescue further supports that Gpr132 is an essential mediator of macrophage PPARγ regulation of breast cancer progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic rescue experiment shown in Figure 5N.

claim: si-Gpr132 significantly reduced tumor volume compared with si-Ctrl.
source: The results showed that si-Gpr132 significantly reduced tumor volume compared with si-Ctrl (Figure 5O), as the result of depleted Gpr132 expression (Figure 5P) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 5O.

claim: si-Gpr132 treatment depleted Gpr132 expression in tumors.
source: The results showed that si-Gpr132 significantly reduced tumor volume compared with si-Ctrl (Figure 5O), as the result of depleted Gpr132 expression (Figure 5P) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-QPCR and western blot data shown in Figure 5P and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Body weight was unaltered by si-Gpr132, indicating a lack of overt toxicity by Gpr132 inhibition.
source: Body weight was unaltered by si-Gpr132 (not shown), indicating a lack of overt toxicity by Gpr132 inhibition.
evidence: This is stated by the authors based on data not shown.

claim: Gpr132 inhibition is a novel anti-cancer strategy.
source: These results support the Gpr132 inhibition as a novel anti-cancer strategy.
evidence: This is inferred from the siRNA knockdown data showing reduced tumor growth.

claim: Macrophage PPARγ plays a crucial yet previously unrecognized role in suppressing cancer progression and mediating the anti-tumor effects of rosiglitazone.
source: Here we have uncovered a crucial yet previously unrecognized role of macrophage PPARγ in suppressing cancer progression and mediating the anti-tumor effects of rosiglitazone (Figure 5Q).
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: PPARγ activation in macrophages tunes down inflammatory programs by repressing the transcription of Gpr132, which is a pro-inflammatory membrane receptor.
source: Mechanistically, PPARγ activation in macrophages tunes down inflammatory programs by repressing the transcription of a novel target gene Gpr132, which is a pro-inflammatory membrane receptor (Figure 5Q).
evidence: This is a summary of the mechanistic findings supported by multiple experiments.

claim: Tumor growth is inhibited when the macrophage Gpr132 level is low by either Gpr132 deletion/inhibition or PPARγ activation via rosiglitazone.
source: Consequently, tumor growth is inhibited when the macrophage Gpr132 level is low by either Gpr132 deletion/inhibition or PPARγ activation via rosiglitazone; whereas tumor growth is exacerbated when the macrophage Gpr132 level is high as the result of macrophage PPARγ deficiency.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings supported by multiple experiments.

claim: Tumor growth is exacerbated when the macrophage Gpr132 level is high as the result of macrophage PPARγ deficiency.
source: Consequently, tumor growth is inhibited when the macrophage Gpr132 level is low by either Gpr132 deletion/inhibition or PPARγ activation via rosiglitazone; whereas tumor growth is exacerbated when the macrophage Gpr132 level is high as the result of macrophage PPARγ deficiency.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings supported by multiple experiments.

claim: Gpr132 is an essential mediator of PPARγ functions in macrophages and tumor progression.
source: Importantly, Gpr132 deletion abolishes the cancer regulation by macrophage PPARγ or rosiglitazone, indicating that Gpr132 is an essential mediator of PPARγ functions in macrophages and tumor progression.
evidence: This is supported by the genetic rescue and pharmacological experiments.

claim: PPARγ and Gpr132 are fundamental key players in TAM.
source: These findings reveal PPARγ and Gpr132 as fundamental key players in TAM, providing new mechanisms how macrophages interact with tumor cells to promote cancer malignancy.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the findings in the manuscript.

claim: Macrophage PPARγ not only regulates cancer cell behavior but also may modulate tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) to alter immune surveillance.
source: Among the many downstream events that mediate the pro-tumor effects of inflammatory macrophages, it is possible that macrophage PPARγ not only regulates cancer cell behavior but also modulates tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) to alter immune surveillance (Engblom et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to Engblom et al., 2016.

claim: PPARγ may act on several cell types to exert anti-tumor effects including cancer cells and immune cells.
source: PPARγ may act on several cell types to exert anti-tumor effects including previously described cancer cells (Mueller et al., 1998; Srivastava et al., 2014; Tontonoz et al., 1997) and now reported immune cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by citations and the current findings.

claim: Macrophage is a key cell type that is essential for the tumor suppressive effects of TZDs.
source: Our findings reveal macrophage as a key cell type, if not the only cell type, that is essential for the tumor suppressive effects of TZDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that rosiglitazone's anti-tumor effects require macrophage PPARγ.

claim: Gpr132 is a very important part of the puzzle and an essential mediator of macrophage PPARγ regulation, because in the absence of Gpr132, the tumor-modulating function of macrophage PPARγ or rosiglitazone is abolished.
source: Nonetheless, our genetic rescue and pharmacological experiments indicate that Gpr132 is a very important part of the puzzle and an essential mediator of macrophage PPARγ regulation, because in the absence of Gpr132, the tumor-modulating function of macrophage PPARγ or rosiglitazone is abolished.
evidence: This is supported by the genetic rescue and pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5L-N.

claim: Gpr132 is a novel key PPARγ target and a new cancer therapeutic target.
source: This uncovers Gpr132 as not only a novel key PPARγ target but also a new cancer therapeutic target.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the findings in the manuscript.

claim: PPARγ directly suppresses the transcriptional activity from Gpr132 promoter.
source: Our luciferase reporter assays indicate that PPARγ directly suppresses the transcriptional activity from Gpr132 promoter, which is further supported by ChIP assays showing PPARγ binding to Gpr132 promoter, leading to a decreased level of H3K9Ac active transcription histone mark at the Gpr132 transcriptional start site.
evidence: This is supported by reporter assays and ChIP assays shown in Figure 3H-J.

claim: Additional mechanisms such as changes in mRNA stability may also contribute to PPARγ down-regulation of Gpr132 mRNA level.
source: Nonetheless, additional mechanisms such as changes in mRNA stability may also contribute to PPARγ down-regulation of Gpr132 mRNA level.
evidence: This is speculation about possible additional mechanisms.

claim: Targeting the infiltrating macrophages to alter their number and properties can lead to a significant inhibition of cancer malignancy.
source: As such, targeting the infiltrating macrophages to alter their number and properties can lead to a significant inhibition of cancer malignancy.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings showing that macrophage modulation affects tumor growth.

claim: Macrophage levels of PPARγ and Gpr132 may predict not only tumor aggressiveness but also the pharmacological responses to rosiglitazone or Gpr132 inhibitors.
source: For example, macrophage levels of PPARγ and Gpr132 may predict not only tumor aggressiveness but also the pharmacological responses to rosiglitazone or Gpr132 inhibitors.
evidence: This is speculation about potential clinical applications.

claim: Cancers with abundant PPARγ-positive macrophages may be sensitive to rosiglitazone whereas cancers with limited macrophages or PPARγ-negative macrophages may be resistant.
source: Our findings may explain why rosiglitazone exerts anti-tumor effects in certain cancers but not others – cancers with abundant PPARγ-positive macrophages may be sensitive whereas cancers with limited macrophages or PPARγ-negative macrophages may be resistant.
evidence: This is speculation to explain variable clinical responses to rosiglitazone.

claim: The positive association of Gpr132 with inflammation and breast cancer in human highlights the exciting potential of Gpr132 blockade as a new therapeutic.
source: Remarkably, the positive association of Gpr132 with inflammation and breast cancer in human (Figure 4B–F), the repression of Gpr132 expression by rosiglitazone in human macrophage (Figure 4A) and the anti-tumor effects of pharmacological Gpr132 inhibition (Figure 5O–P) highlight the exciting potential of Gpr132 blockade as a new therapeutic.
evidence: This is inferred from the human data and pharmacological inhibition experiments.

claim: Gpr132 expression is significantly increased in the majority of human breast cancers.
source: Moreover, the observation that Gpr132 expression is significantly increased in the majority of human breast cancers (Figure 4B) suggests that Gpr132 may serve as a useful marker for breast cancer prognosis, similar to the 21 genes typically examined in the commercially available Oncotype Dx panel.
evidence: This is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Gpr132 may serve as a useful marker for breast cancer prognosis.
source: Moreover, the observation that Gpr132 expression is significantly increased in the majority of human breast cancers (Figure 4B) suggests that Gpr132 may serve as a useful marker for breast cancer prognosis, similar to the 21 genes typically examined in the commercially available Oncotype Dx panel.
evidence: This is speculation based on the increased Gpr132 expression in human breast cancers.

claim: Macrophage is an important cell type that contributes to PPARγ suppression of cancer and the anti-tumor effects of rosiglitazone.
source: In summary, the significance of our findings resides in the following aspects: (1) it reveals macrophage as an important cell type that contributes to PPARγ suppression of cancer and the anti-tumor effects of rosiglitazone; (2) it identifies Gpr132 as a novel PPARγ direct target gene in macrophages that mediates PPARγ functions; (3) it uncovers Gpr132 as a pro-inflammatory and pro-tumor factor in macrophages, and thus a novel therapeutic target.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings.

claim: Gpr132 is a novel PPARγ direct target gene in macrophages that mediates PPARγ functions.
source: In summary, the significance of our findings resides in the following aspects: (1) it reveals macrophage as an important cell type that contributes to PPARγ suppression of cancer and the anti-tumor effects of rosiglitazone; (2) it identifies Gpr132 as a novel PPARγ direct target gene in macrophages that mediates PPARγ functions; (3) it uncovers Gpr132 as a pro-inflammatory and pro-tumor factor in macrophages, and thus a novel therapeutic target.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings.

claim: Gpr132 is a pro-inflammatory and pro-tumor factor in macrophages, and thus a novel therapeutic target.
source: In summary, the significance of our findings resides in the following aspects: (1) it reveals macrophage as an important cell type that contributes to PPARγ suppression of cancer and the anti-tumor effects of rosiglitazone; (2) it identifies Gpr132 as a novel PPARγ direct target gene in macrophages that mediates PPARγ functions; (3) it uncovers Gpr132 as a pro-inflammatory and pro-tumor factor in macrophages, and thus a novel therapeutic target.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings.
